title: Anxiety
hookLine: be not solicitous, and also be gentle with a worried mind
tomorrow: who takes care of the person taking care of everyone?

cards: Two in the morning, heart going fast, the mind rehearsing a phone call that hasn't happened yet. Then a second layer: somewhere there's a verse that says don't worry, so now you're worried about worrying.
Is anxiety a sin? The short answer from this tradition is no. The night before he died, Jesus himself began to fear.

teach.b: Mark says it of the garden of Gethsemane, in the Douay-Rheims: "he began to fear and to be heavy." Fear isn't a failure of faith if Jesus felt it. So what does the well-known line mean?
"Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow; for the morrow will be solicitous for itself. Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof." Solicitous is the old word for anxious.
It reads less like a scolding than an invitation: leave tomorrow where it is. And notice what Jesus does just before, in the same sermon. He points at things you can see.
Birds that don't store food in barns.
"Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." He sends a worried mind to the senses. Look.
Breathe. One to tell a friend: on the night he was afraid, Jesus didn't go off alone.
He asked three friends to stay and keep watch with him.
Being gentle with fear means that: you don't shame it, you don't obey it, and you don't sit with it alone. And when worry becomes a weight that won't lift, yesterday's line still holds. Help is holy.

how: Catholics bring worry to prayer, often with Matthew 6 or a slow, breath-paced prayer, and are encouraged to seek care when anxiety is heavy; in danger, 988 in the US or local emergency help.

o: a lack of faith that must be confessed
fear that runs ahead into tomorrow
the calm that comes from trusting God

games.q: your younger cousin panics before a test and says, 'I'm a bad Christian, the Bible says don't worry.' what's the gentle answer from today?
o: Jesus felt fear too. let's breathe, and leave tomorrow for tomorrow.
you're right; if you trusted God more, you wouldn't feel this.
just ignore the verse; it wasn't written about tests anyway.
games.why: Jesus began to fear in Gethsemane. 'be not solicitous' invites, it doesn't shame: be gentle with fear, and don't sit with it alone.

practice: Sit back and rest one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and let each breath out run a little longer than the breath in. With every breath out, set tomorrow down on the shelf where it belongs.
If you pray, you can pray as you breathe, with the words sufficient for the day.

wordCard.voice: Anxiety. Fear that runs ahead into tomorrow. Jesus felt fear too, and this tradition meets it with gentleness, not shame. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to be anxious, pulled in many directions. the verb behind 'be not solicitous'.

carryVoice: The line to keep: be gentle with fear, and leave tomorrow for tomorrow. See you then.
